Don't really think this is necessary. Trivial to do already:
   `Key.get(key.getTypeLiteral(), annotation)`

It was to provide the opposite of `Key#ofType` which makes sense to have as it deals with the `AnnotationStrategy` itself.

There's not a huge difference with changing the annotation, one just involves less duplication:
`key.withAnnotation(annotation)`
`Key.get(key.getTypeLiteral(), annotation)`

If you don't think this is necessary, that's fine - feel free to close.
ofType is slightly more necessary, as construction a new variant with a different type requires some branching (to deal with annotation instances vs annotation types).

Personally, the discoverability here is at least a bit of a selling point. More than once I've looked for an `ofType()` sibling for annotations in `Key` and realized I need to instead use the factory method.
if you think it's worth it extra methods, feel free to merge in.

Any chance of getting this in soon? :smiley_cat:
Is there a chance of this getting in soon?
I'll take a swing at it over the long weekend :)
Thank you! :smile:
Thanks for the contribution, and your patience :)

@mveitas thanks for the contribution! We actually have an internal class that does the same thing as your proposed module, though we've hesitated to open-source it since it takes advantage of (presently) undocumented behavior.

I would suggest filing a bug asking to add such a class to Guice, then we can evaluate whether that makes sense. The change itself is small, but choosing to make this implementation detail part of the contract is a bigger question.

It's worth noting that a version of this class exists in quite a few projects that use Guice.
A couple examples:
- Governator: [here](https://github.com/Netflix/governator/blob/master/governator-core/src/main/java/com/netflix/governator/SingletonModule.java) and [here](https://github.com/Netflix/governator/blob/master/governator-legacy/src/main/java/com/netflix/governator/guice/SingletonModule.java)
- [guice-dedupe](https://github.com/fzakaria/guide-dedupe/blob/master/src/main/java/com/github/fzakaria/guice/dedupe/SingletonModule.java) (http://blog.fzakaria.com/2016/12/11/large-scale-guice-projects-module-deduplication/)

Speaking as a Governator owner, @dimo414 is correct in that this implementation does raise some larger questions. The behavior of this in combination with Modules.override for example is poorly defined. I'd definitely +1 for a solution to this issue, but this implementation by itself feels incomplete.

@pshirshov, there's nothing I can say to remove the frustration of years of radio silence.

Guice, by and large, is a stable and "finished" project. It's a backbone of millions (if not billions) of QPS within Google, and does its job well enough. As a result, there's little priority given to its evolution. Changes (when they do happen) tend to be in the form of "add handcuffs", as opposed to "enable more", because we've found its flexibility is also its greatest poison.

As to why I've suddenly shown up after years of silence... in light of [@crazybob's passing](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=35457341), I wanted to do _something_ to honor Bob's memory. I was incredibly lucky to have been able to engage with Bob & others during the early stages of Guice's life, and it's unfortunate that we've let Guice's community stagnate over the years. It seemed like scrubbing the open PRs and issues was the least I could do.

As to your specific question of how to land such a change: I think the best way would be to show how this concept has no possible workaround, how lack of it causes significant problems, and how incorporating it won't prevent developers from making sense of their object graph & dependencies.

Eh, if this conversation happens back in 2017 I would show and explain, now I have zero motivation for this.

Still, I would like to add a couple of crticial comments. 

1. I'm not sure why you call Guice "flexible", it won't allow me to resolve the problem described in #1128  nor, for example, dump a graphviz file effectlessly.
2. It doesn't matter how widely a library is adopted if it's outdated and badly designed. In my opinion, Guice promotes extremely outdated practices, is extremely badly designed (too ad-hoc; no planning; too many things happen just in time; no resource management; too many things happen in runtime; no proper support for resource/lifecycle management, memoization, context inheritance; invasive; nondetermenistic; unpredictable outside of happy paths; no sane conflict resolution; laziness instead of graph roots) and poorly implemented (unmaintainable overcoupled code full of singletons). A proper theory (project networks) allows to implement orders of magnitude more sound and determenistic DI.
2. I'm wondering how the world where Google won't use a subpar and extremely imperfect tech as one of the cornerstones would look like.

What's the motivation for this PR? Is Guice not working in your project? Guice is intentionally still on Java 8 in order to support such users.
hi. I see many other opensource projects using Guice. They are moving on java 10, so they are forced to delete Guice as dependency unless Guice move to java 10 too

> they are forced to delete Guice as dependency unless Guice move to java 10 too

Can you share some concrete examples of this? We are not aware of any such limitation, and it's unlikely that upgrading Guice to Java 10 (which *would* break all projects that haven't updated) is the appropriate fix. There should be no problem with a Java 10 project depending on Guice.

An example is Lightbend's Lagom Framework: it is based on Play! Framework, which uses Guice. It is stuck on Java 8 until these problems are sorted out. They have recently decided to jump directly to 11 (citing Cassandra's team same decision).

Work on Guice for JDK 10/11 seems ongoing here:
https://github.com/google/guice/pull/1169

Relevant discussions:
https://github.com/playframework/playframework/issues/8454
https://github.com/lagom/lagom/issues/1276
https://github.com/lagom/lagom/issues/1417

Thanks to all the contributors for their work!
Thanks for the cross-reference @michelemauro - #1169 is definitely a more appropriate fix than updating Guice wholesale.

original_comments: we should add a TODO that when we drop jdk8 support we can rm this 'else' branch, because its only needed as a fallback since using reflection wasn't a reliable way to do things.

OOC, in what ways does findSpecial differ from unreflectSpecial?   are the two functionally equivalent (ignoring the JDK bugs), except one stards with reflect data (Method) and the other with a signature (MethodType)?

if so, is it worthwhile simplifying this to _just_ use findSpecial?

also: does this change have any impact on the calculus of who has access?  if the types (args or return) are private, package-private or protected, will unreflectSpecial|findSpecial fail whereas the reflected approach would have succeeded, because we explicitly set the modes to all access levels?

`unreflectSpecial` is intended to be equivalent to `findSpecial` but slightly faster because it avoids an extra resolution step. (The JVM can re-use detail in the reflected method so it doesn't need to match the given name+type signature against potential candidates.) It also skips security checks which have already been performed during reflection.

Just using `findSpecial` would save one call to `unreflectSpecial` at the cost of always re-resolving default methods on Java14+... note it would only save one call because if `unreflectSpecial` fails then we remember that and avoid trying it again.

I'm tempted to leave it in because I don't think removing it would simplify the code that much - we'd still want to remember falling back to the private lookup if/when that happens because otherwise we'd penalise Java8 users by always attempting a different approach even when we knew it would never work. (That's if we still follow the same general pattern - did you have a different suggestion?)

Regarding access, since this PR always falls back to the `privateLookup` approach if all of the other approaches fail then this shouldn't change existing behaviour. What it does do is avoid the `privateLookup` if any of the other approaches succeed first (which is more likely on recent JDKs.)

If leaving it in if it makes a difference (even it's just a single resolution step), then keeping it makes sense to me.

Insofar as falling back to privateLookup because of access issues... that makes less sense to me, particularly because the fallback mechanism is static.  So if using unreflectSpecial|findSpecial fails for non-public members, then if you have just a single non-public usage in your code, you can expect all your code to ultimately be using the reflection-based approach and continuing to receive the warnings about that.

That's not to say that I think we should use try the tiered approach every time... but it does make me wonder about the utility of it  (Also because the fallback in the PR is using only jdk8 constructor params, so I think it would end up failing on later JDKs.)

Fundamentally we either take a versioned approach, using the JDK version to decide what to do - or we take a behaviour-based approach, starting with the available public API and falling back to internal API when that fails. Because it would be expensive to continually fall-through the different approaches on Java 8, this PR caches (statically) which approach worked for all the scenarios so far.

IMHO this is reasonable because if we've fallen through to use the private lookup then it's likely this will happen again. At that point we've already done the hard bit (looking up the constructor and making it accessible) so re-using the now accessible constructor is simple and doesn't trigger further warnings. In other words since we've got access to it we might as well skip straight to it.

Also in this case we know we're dealing with public methods, because default methods are always public. This coupled with the `unreflectSpecial` fixes in Java 14+ means that approach works even when the interface itself is private. If the JVM is older then we fall back to `findSpecial` which works for Java9+ even when the interface itself is private. Finally for Java8 we fall back to the internal API.

Regarding the different `Lookup` constructor, that appeared in Java14 - so far I haven't found a situation where `unreflectSpecial` fails on Java14 even for private interfaces, but I haven't tested all JPMS scenarios. But we can easily add support for the Java14+ Lookup constructor just in case. The alternative would be to grab the trusted `IMPL_LOOKUP` field, but that feels more risky.
